Electrons flow **into** the body, so the body must have been short of them - it was
**positively charged**.
**Step 1 — recall what earthing does.** Connecting a body to earth lets charge flow
until the body reaches earth's potential, taken as **zero** ✓
**Step 2 — read the direction of flow.** Electrons move **from the earth into the
body** ✓ The body was therefore **deficient** in electrons.
**Step 3 — conclude.** A deficiency of electrons means a **positive** charge, so before
earthing the body was **charged positively** ✓
**Why electrons and not protons move.** In a solid conductor only the **electrons** are
mobile ✓ The positive ions are fixed in the lattice. All charge transfer in metals is
carried out by electrons, so a body is made positive by **removing** electrons, never
by adding protons.
**The direction rule, worth fixing.**
electrons flow **into** the body → the body was **positive** ✓
electrons flow **out of** the body → the body was **negative** ✓
Note that the conventional **current** flows the opposite way to the electrons in each
case.
**What the body becomes afterwards.** **Neutral**, at earth potential ✓ Earth is an
effectively infinite reservoir of charge, so it supplies or absorbs whatever is needed
without changing its own potential measurably.
**Why earthing matters in practice.** It prevents dangerous charge accumulation ✓
Metal appliance cases are earthed so that a fault cannot raise them to a lethal
potential; fuel tankers trail an earthing strap so that static cannot spark; and
lightning conductors give the charge a safe path.
**The subtlety of earthing a charged conductor.** It is not that "charge flows to
earth" in some vague sense - the flow is in whichever **direction** neutralises the
body ✓ A negatively charged body sends electrons **to** earth; a positive one draws
them **from** earth, as here.
**A related case - earthing by induction.** Bring a positive rod near an insulated
sphere and earth the far side ✓ Electrons flow **up** into the sphere, and on removing
the earth connection the sphere is left **negatively** charged - charged by induction,
with the opposite sign to the rod.
**Reading the distractors.** **Uncharged** ✗ would need no flow at all. **Charged
negatively** ✗ would send electrons the other way. **An insulator** ✗ could not conduct
the charge in the first place ✓
∴ charged positively.

Both neighbours **attract** B, since all three currents are parallel - and C's pull is
the stronger.
**Step 1 — recall the rule.** Parallel currents in the **same** direction **attract**;
opposite ones repel ✓ All three wires here carry current the same way, so A and C both
**attract** B.
**Step 2 — compute each force per unit length.**
F/L = **2 x 10⁻⁷ I₁I₂/d** ✓
from A: 2 x 10⁻⁷(1)(2)/d = **4 x 10⁻⁷/d**, directed **towards A** ✓
from C: 2 x 10⁻⁷(2)(3)/d = **12 x 10⁻⁷/d**, directed **towards C** ✓
**Step 3 — take the resultant.** The two pull in opposite directions:
net = (12 − 4) x 10⁻⁷/d = **8 x 10⁻⁷/d**, directed **towards C** ✓
**Why C wins.** It carries **three times** A's current at the **same** distance ✓ so its
pull is three times as strong, and the net force points towards it.
**Where the force would vanish.** Only if the currents were in the ratio of the
distances ✓ With equal distances, equal currents in A and C would balance exactly. Here
1 A against 3 A cannot.
**Why the force is in the plane of the paper.** Each force is **perpendicular** to both
the current and the other wire's field ✓ The fields are into or out of the page at B,
and the current in B is in the plane, so the force lies in the plane too - which rules
out the two "perpendicular to the paper" options at once.
**Why parallel currents attract.** Wire A's field at B points into the page, and
F̄ = I L̄ x B̄ with the current downward gives a force **towards A** ✓ The result is
general: like currents pull together, which is why the coils of a solenoid squeeze
themselves and why a lightning strike can crush a hollow conductor.
**The definition of the ampere.** Framed in terms of exactly this force ✓ Two infinite
parallel wires a metre apart carrying one ampere each attract with 2 x 10⁻⁷ N per
metre - the historical definition, superseded in 2019 by a fixed value of e.
**A numerical instance.** With d = 1 cm:
from A: 4 x 10⁻⁵ N m⁻¹
from C: 1·2 x 10⁻⁴ N m⁻¹ ✓
net 8 x 10⁻⁵ N m⁻¹ towards C.
**Reading the distractors.** **Towards A** ✗ reverses the comparison. The two
**perpendicular to the paper** options ✗ are geometrically impossible for forces
between coplanar parallel wires ✓
∴ towards C.

At totality the photosphere is hidden and the chromosphere alone is seen - giving a
bright **line emission** spectrum.
**Step 1 — recall the normal solar spectrum.** The hot, dense **photosphere** gives a
**continuous** spectrum, crossed by dark **Fraunhofer** lines where the cooler gases
above it absorb ✓ That is a **line absorption** spectrum.
**Step 2 — see what totality changes.** The Moon covers the photosphere, removing the
continuous background ✓ Only the thin **chromosphere** remains visible, glowing at the
edge of the disc.
**Step 3 — see what a hot thin gas emits.** **Bright lines** at exactly the wavelengths
it would otherwise absorb ✓ So the spectrum becomes a **line emission** spectrum.
**Why it is called the flash spectrum.** It appears for only a **few seconds**, just as
totality begins and again as it ends ✓ The dark Fraunhofer lines "flash" into bright
emission lines and back again - one of the most striking sights in observational
astronomy.
**Kirchhoff's law at work.** A gas emits strongly at exactly the wavelengths it
absorbs ✓ Seen **against** the bright photosphere, the chromosphere's lines appear
**dark**; seen against the **dark sky**, the same lines appear **bright**. Nothing about
the gas has changed - only the background.
**The historical discovery.** In the eclipse of **1868**, Janssen and Lockyer found a
yellow line in the flash spectrum matching no known element ✓ They named the element
**helium**, after the Greek for Sun. It was not found on Earth until 1895 - the only
element discovered in space before being discovered here.
**The three kinds of spectrum, distinguished.**
**continuous**: hot dense solid, liquid or gas - the photosphere ✓
**line emission**: hot rarefied gas - the chromosphere, a discharge tube ✓
**line absorption**: cool gas in front of a continuous source - the ordinary solar
spectrum ✓
**Why this matters for astronomy.** Spectra reveal **composition, temperature, density,
magnetic field and radial velocity** ✓ Nearly everything known about the stars comes
from analysing their light this way.
**Reading the distractors.** **Continuous emission** ✗ is the photosphere, now hidden.
**Line absorption** ✗ is the ordinary uneclipsed spectrum. **Band absorption** ✗ comes
from **molecules**, as in cool stars and planetary atmospheres ✓
∴ line emission spectrum.

Heavy water is **D₂O** - the oxide of **deuterium**.
**Step 1 — identify deuterium.** It is the **heavy isotope of hydrogen**, ²₁H, whose
nucleus contains **one proton and one neutron** ✓ against ordinary hydrogen's lone
proton.
**Step 2 — form the compound.** Two deuterium atoms with one oxygen give **D₂O**, a
**compound of deuterium and oxygen** ✓
**Why it is "heavy".** Its molar mass is **20 g mol⁻¹** against ordinary water's 18 ✓
about 11% heavier, and its density is 1·105 g cm⁻³ - so an ice cube of heavy water
**sinks** in ordinary water.
**Where it occurs.** About **1 part in 6400** of natural water ✓ and it is separated by
repeated electrolysis or distillation, which is laborious and expensive.
**Its great technological use.** As a **moderator** in nuclear reactors ✓ It slows fast
neutrons to thermal energies while absorbing very few of them - far fewer than ordinary
water does. That low absorption lets a reactor run on **natural uranium**, without
enrichment, which is the basis of the Canadian CANDU design and India's pressurised
heavy-water reactors.
**Why ordinary water is a poorer moderator.** Ordinary hydrogen **captures** neutrons
to form deuterium ✓ so a light-water reactor loses too many neutrons and needs
**enriched** fuel to sustain the chain reaction.
**Its other properties.** It freezes at **3·8 °C** and boils at **101·4 °C** ✓ slightly
higher than ordinary water, because the heavier atoms vibrate more slowly and its
hydrogen bonds are a little stronger.
**Is it toxic?** Mildly, in quantity ✓ Replacing a large fraction of an organism's water
disrupts cell division, because reaction rates involving D-O bonds are measurably
slower. A glass of it would do no harm; living on it would.
**Why option 2 is wrong even though it sounds right.** "Heavy oxygen **and** heavy
hydrogen" ✗ - heavy water contains **ordinary** oxygen-16 ✓ Only the hydrogen is
isotopically substituted. Water made with oxygen-18 exists and is used as a tracer, but
it is not what "heavy water" means.
**Reading the other distractors.** "**Water in which soap does not lather**" ✗ is
**hard** water, containing calcium and magnesium salts - an entirely different idea
that the similar name invites. "**Water at 4 °C**" ✗ is merely water at its density
maximum ✓
∴ compound of deuterium and oxygen.

Young's modulus is a **stress**, so its units are those of **pressure** - and
**N m⁻¹** is not among them.
**Step 1 — recall the definition.**
Y = stress/strain = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) ✓
Strain is **dimensionless**, so Y has the units of **stress**: force per unit area.
**Step 2 — test each option.**
**N m⁻²** ✓ force per area - correct, and the SI unit
**dyne cm⁻²** ✓ the CGS equivalent; 1 N m⁻² = 10 dyne cm⁻²
**megapascal** ✓ 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻², so MPa = 10⁶ N m⁻² - correct, and the unit engineers
actually use
**N m⁻¹** ✗ force per **length**, not per area - **not** a unit of Young's modulus ✓
**What N m⁻¹ actually measures.** A **spring constant**, F = kx ✓ or a **surface
tension**, force per unit length of a line in the surface. Both are force per length,
and neither is a stress.
**Typical values of Y.**
steel: **2 x 10¹¹ Pa = 200 GPa** ✓
copper: 110 GPa
glass: 60 GPa
rubber: about **10⁶ Pa = 1 MPa** - a hundred thousand times smaller, which is why it
stretches so visibly ✓
**Why engineers use megapascals.** The pascal is inconveniently small ✓ A steel cable's
working stress is around 200 MPa, a much more manageable number than 2 x 10⁸ Pa.
**The dimensional formula.**
[Y] = [M L⁻¹ T⁻²] ✓ the same as pressure, energy density and the bulk and rigidity
moduli.
**The quick test for such questions.** Strain is a **pure number**, so the modulus must
carry the units of **stress** ✓ Anything that is not force per area is wrong, and
N m⁻¹ fails at once.
**Why the question is worth asking.** The similarity of N m⁻¹ and N m⁻² catches the
careless ✓ and the distinction between a **spring constant** (property of an object)
and a **modulus** (property of a material) is a genuine conceptual one.
∴ Nm⁻¹.

The two neighbours push wire C **equally and oppositely**, so the net force is
**zero**.
**Step 1 — read the arrangement.** The middle wire carries **10 A**, with a **30 A**
wire 3 cm to one side and a **20 A** wire 2 cm to the other, both carrying current
**opposite** to the middle one ✓
**Step 2 — compute each force on a 25 cm length.**
F = 2 x 10⁻⁷ (I₁I₂/d) L ✓
from the 30 A wire:
2 x 10⁻⁷ x (30 x 10)/0·03 x 0·25
= 2 x 10⁻⁷ x 10⁴ x 0·25
= **5 x 10⁻⁴ N** ✓
from the 20 A wire:
2 x 10⁻⁷ x (10 x 20)/0·02 x 0·25
= 2 x 10⁻⁷ x 10⁴ x 0·25
= **5 x 10⁻⁴ N** ✓
**Step 3 — take the resultant.** Both are **repulsive**, since each outer current
opposes the middle one, so they push C in **opposite** directions ✓
net force = 5 x 10⁻⁴ − 5 x 10⁻⁴ = **zero** ✓
**Why the two balance so exactly.** The nearer wire carries **less** current, and the
further one **more**, in just the right proportion ✓
30/3 = **10** and 20/2 = **10**
The quantity I/d is the same for both, and that is precisely what the force depends on.
**The balance condition in general.** The middle wire feels no force when
**I₁/d₁ = I₂/d₂** ✓ Here 30/3 = 20/2 = 10, so the arrangement is in equilibrium.
**Why opposite currents repel.** F̄ = I L̄ x B̄ with the field reversed gives a force
**outward** ✓ The rule is the mirror of the attraction between parallel currents, and
it is why the two halves of a hairpin conductor fly apart.
**Is the equilibrium stable?** No ✓ Displace C slightly towards the 30 A wire and its
repulsion grows as 1/d while the other's weakens - pushing C further away. It is an
**unstable** equilibrium.
**Why the 25 cm length matters.** The force is proportional to the length ✓ It would
scale any non-zero answer, but here both contributions carry the same factor and cancel
regardless.
**Reading the distractors.** **10⁻³ N** ✗ is the **sum** of the two, which would be
right only if both pushed the same way - that is, if the outer currents were in
**opposite** senses to each other. **2·5 x 10⁻³** and **1·5 x 10⁻³ N** ✗ match no
combination ✓
∴ zero.

Combine the **amplitudes**, not the intensities, then square.
**Step 1 — convert intensities to amplitudes.** Since I ∝ A²:
a₁ ∝ √I
a₂ ∝ √(4I) = **2√I** ✓
**Step 2 — find the extreme amplitudes.**
constructive: a₁ + a₂ = **3√I**
destructive: a₂ − a₁ = **√I** ✓
**Step 3 — square to get the intensities.**
I_max = (3√I)² = **9I** ✓
I_min = (√I)² = **I** ✓
**The standard formulas.**
I_max = (√I₁ + √I₂)² ✓
I_min = (√I₁ − √I₂)² ✓
**Why the amplitudes and not the intensities add.** Waves superpose by adding their
**displacements** ✓ Intensity is proportional to the **square** of the resultant
amplitude, so it must be computed last. Adding I + 4I = 5I - which is one of the
distractors - treats light as though it did not interfere at all.
**Where the energy goes.** The average of the maximum and minimum is
(9I + I)/2 = **5I** ✓ exactly the sum of the two beams. Interference **redistributes**
energy between bright and dark fringes; it never creates or destroys it.
**The fringe visibility.**
V = (I_max − I_min)/(I_max + I_min) = 8I/10I = **0·8** ✓ high contrast, though not
perfect - complete darkness in the dark fringes requires **equal** intensities.
**Why equal intensities give the best fringes.** Then I_min = (√I − √I)² = **0** ✓ and
the visibility is 1. Unequal beams always leave some light in the minima, which is why
a beam splitter in an interferometer is made as close to 50 : 50 as possible.
**A check on the ratio.** I_max/I_min = 9 ✓ and the general result is
[(√I₂ + √I₁)/(√I₂ − √I₁)]² = (3/1)² = 9 ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **5I and 3I** ✗ and **5I and I** ✗ both add the
intensities somewhere. **9I and 3I** ✗ gets the maximum right but squares the
difference wrongly ✓
∴ 9 I and I.

An alpha particle has **twice** the charge and **four times** the mass, so its specific
charge is **half** the proton's.
**Step 1 — write the specific charge of each.**
proton: q/m = **e/m_p** = 9·6 x 10⁷ C kg⁻¹ ✓
alpha: an alpha is a helium nucleus, **2 protons + 2 neutrons**, so
q = **2e** and m ≈ **4m_p** ✓
**Step 2 — form the ratio.**
(q/m)_alpha = 2e/(4m_p)
= **(1/2)(e/m_p)** ✓
**Step 3 — compute.**
= 9·6 x 10⁷/2
= **4·8 x 10⁷ C kg⁻¹** ✓
**Why the mass wins over the charge.** The charge doubles but the mass **quadruples** ✓
so the ratio is halved. Doubling the charge alone would have doubled the specific
charge; the extra two neutrons more than undo it.
**Why specific charge matters.** It is what determines a particle's behaviour in
electric and magnetic fields ✓
a = qE/m for an electric field
r = mv/(qB) = v/[(q/m)B] for a magnetic one
Two particles with the same q/m follow **identical** paths at the same speed, whatever
their individual charge and mass.
**A comparison across particles.**
electron: **1·76 x 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹** ✓ - some 1836 times the proton's
proton: **9·6 x 10⁷** ✓
deuteron: **4·8 x 10⁷** - same as an alpha, since 1 charge and 2 mass units ✓
alpha: **4·8 x 10⁷** ✓
**Why the deuteron and alpha coincide.** Both have mass numbers exactly twice their
charge numbers ✓ so they are indistinguishable to a mass spectrometer - a real
experimental nuisance, resolved only by precise mass measurement.
**How specific charge is measured.** By **Thomson's method** with crossed fields, or
from the radius of curvature in a magnetic field ✓ The electron's value was the first
to be found, in 1897.
**A caution on the mass.** Strictly the alpha's mass is **3·97** proton masses, not 4,
because of the nuclear binding energy ✓ The 0·8% difference is below the precision of
these options.
**Reading the distractors.** **19·2 x 10⁷** ✗ doubles instead of halving - counting the
charge but not the mass. **9·6 x 10⁷** ✗ assumes no change, and **2·4 x 10⁷** ✗ divides
by four, counting the mass but not the charge ✓
∴ 4.8 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹.
